children.text: The Money Still Owed

After claims are submitted, paid, and posted, there is always a residual: money that has been billed but not yet collected. That outstanding balance — owed by payers and patients — is accounts receivable (AR). Managing AR is the back-end discipline of systematically chasing that unpaid money until it is collected or appropriately written off.

AR management matters because billed revenue is not collected revenue. A claim can be perfectly submitted and still sit unpaid for weeks because the payer is slow, the claim got stuck, or no one followed up. AR is where revenue goes to wait — and where, without active management, it quietly ages, becomes harder to collect, and eventually dies as bad debt.

The core insight driving all of AR management is that money gets harder to collect the older it gets. Collectibility within the first 60 days runs high — around 90 percent — but once an account passes 90 days, the probability of ever collecting falls dramatically, toward half or less. Time is the enemy, which is why AR is organized entirely around age.

Accounts receivable (AR) is billed-but-uncollected revenue owed by payers and patients. The central truth of AR management: money gets harder to collect the older it gets — collectibility is ~90% within 60 days but falls sharply past 90 days.
Days in AR: The Headline Number

The single most important AR metric is Days in Accounts Receivable — the average number of days it takes to collect after billing. The calculation is straightforward: Total Accounts Receivable divided by Average Daily Charges (total charges over a period divided by the number of days in that period). The result is "how many days of billing is currently sitting uncollected."

Lower is better. The widely used benchmark is to keep Days in AR under 40 (per HFMA and MGMA norms), with leading organizations under 30. A rising Days in AR is one of the earliest warning signs that something is wrong upstream — claims are being denied, delayed, or not followed up — because all of that backs up into uncollected receivables.

Days in AR is powerful precisely because it is a summary number that reflects the health of the whole cycle. You cannot fix it directly; you fix it by fixing the things that feed it — cleaner claims, faster denial work, diligent follow-up. It is the thermometer, not the disease.

children.text: Aging Buckets: Organizing AR by Time

Because age determines collectibility, AR is organized into "aging buckets" — groupings of receivables by how long they have been outstanding. The standard buckets are 0-30, 31-60, 61-90, 91-120, and 120+ days, each showing the dollar amount sitting in it. The AR aging report is the back-end's primary worklist and dashboard.

The aging report instantly reveals the shape of the problem. A healthy AR profile is weighted toward the youngest buckets, with little money in 90+ days. When dollars pile up in the older buckets, it signals that claims are getting stuck and not being worked — and that revenue is sliding toward the point of no return. High performers keep less than about 15 percent of total AR in the 90+ day bucket.

Aging buckets also separate the two kinds of AR: insurance (payer) AR and patient AR. They behave differently — patient balances are generally harder and slower to collect, so a higher tolerance for older self-pay AR is normal. Reading the aging report means looking not just at totals but at where the money sits, who owes it, and which buckets are growing.
The Follow-Up Process

AR follow-up is the systematic work of tracking unpaid claims and balances, contacting payers or patients to resolve them, correcting errors, resubmitting claims, and filing appeals when needed. It is the active, hands-on chasing that turns aged receivables back into cash — and it is organized around the aging buckets.

Effective follow-up assigns staff to specific buckets — someone focused on accounts approaching 60 days, another on the 90-plus accounts — and prioritizes the worklist by both age and dollar value. The principle mirrors denial prioritization: work the highest-value and most time-sensitive accounts first, and document every payer call and response so the follow-up has a trail.

Cadence matters. Most organizations review AR reports at least weekly for operational follow-up, because catching a stuck claim at 35 days and resolving it is vastly better than discovering it at 95 days when it is half-uncollectible. The discipline is to keep accounts moving down toward resolution before they age into the low-collectibility buckets — proactive follow-up rather than reactive cleanup.

children.text: Why Speed Wins

The throughline of AR management is that speed wins, because of the collectibility curve. An account worked in the 31-60 bucket is highly collectible; the same account left to reach 120+ days may be worth a fraction of its face value, even though nothing about the underlying claim changed. The decline is not about the claim's validity — it is purely about elapsed time.

This is why the youngest buckets deserve attention too, not just the old ones. Preventing a claim from aging is cheaper and more effective than rescuing it after it has aged. Strong AR management is therefore front-loaded: catch and resolve issues early, keep the aging report weighted young, and reserve heroic recovery efforts for the genuinely hard cases.

Eventually, some AR is uncollectible and must be written off — but that decision should be deliberate, based on real recovery probability, not the accidental result of neglect. Well-managed AR keeps Days in AR low, the 90+ bucket small, and write-offs intentional. What remains after payer AR is worked is the patient's portion — which is its own distinct challenge, and the subject of the final lesson in this module: patient collections.

body.message: Collectibility falls with age regardless of whether the claim is correct — ~90% within 60 days, dropping sharply past 90 days. Letting accounts drift into older buckets destroys recoverable revenue. Work AR proactively and weekly to keep it young; do not wait until accounts are nearly uncollectible.
